covid-19.name: COVID-19
covid-19.definition: COVID-19 is an illness caused by a virus called coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), with symptoms that overlap with colds and flu.
covid-19.overview: COVID-19 is an infection caused by a virus that spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes. The NHS says its symptoms are very similar to those of other illnesses such as colds and flu. Some people, including older adults, those with weakened immune systems and those with certain long-term conditions, are at higher risk of severe illness, according to WHO. Some people go on to have symptoms that last for a long time, which is called long COVID.
causes: Infection with the virus SARS-CoV-2
Breathing in infectious respiratory particles released when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes
Touching a contaminated surface and then the eyes, nose or mouth
Close contact with an infected person or sharing a closed space with them
riskFactors: Older age
Underlying health conditions such as diabetes, heart or lung disease and obesity
A weakened immune system, including HIV
Pregnancy
Not being vaccinated
signs: A high temperature
Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath in more severe illness, which the CDC lists as an emergency warning sign in adults
complications: Becoming seriously ill, especially in people at higher risk
Pneumonia and sepsis in some people admitted to hospital, as recorded in a US hospital study published by the CDC
Long COVID, with symptoms lasting for weeks or longer
Persistent tiredness, breathlessness, joint pain and aching muscles after the infection
Problems with memory and concentration, often called brain fog
Heart palpitations, dizziness, and anxiety or depression during long COVID
covid-19.diagnosis: The NHS says the symptoms are very similar to those of colds and flu. It also says most people cannot get free rapid lateral flow tests, though some people at highest risk of serious illness can, and that most people with symptoms do not need to take one. For people eligible for COVID-19 treatments, the NHS advises taking a rapid lateral flow test as soon as symptoms start.
covid-19.treatment: The NHS says home measures such as rest, plenty of fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease symptoms. For a cough, it suggests avoiding lying flat on the back and not using a fan to cool the room. The NHS offers antiviral medicines, including nirmatrelvir with ritonavir and molnupiravir, to people at highest risk of becoming seriously ill. The CDC says antiviral treatment has to be started soon after symptoms begin.
covid-19.prevention: Vaccination helps protect against severe illness, and the UK offers a seasonal programme to the groups at highest risk of serious illness. The NHS advises staying at home and away from others when there is a high temperature or a person does not feel well enough to do normal activities.
covid-19.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, coughing up blood, or collapsing. Contact the GP or NHS 111 urgently if symptoms are getting worse or not improving, or if a high temperature lasts five days or more. People at higher risk, such as those who are pregnant, aged 60 or over, or have a weakened immune system, are advised to get medical advice sooner. A routine GP appointment is the route for symptoms that last a long time after the infection.

sections.heading: What is COVID-19 and how does it spread?
sections.body:
COVID-19 is an illness caused by a virus called coronavirus, formally SARS-CoV-2. WHO says the virus spreads through the air in infectious respiratory particles that an infected person releases when breathing, talking, coughing or sneezing. It can also spread when someone touches a contaminated surface and then touches the eyes, nose or mouth.

People are more likely to catch the virus when they are close to an infected person, or when they share a closed space with them. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says that anyone infected can spread the virus even without symptoms, and that people can pass it on before symptoms begin. A CDC travel guide adds that most spread seems to happen early in the infection, particularly in the day or two before symptoms start.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of COVID-19?
sections.body:
The NHS says the symptoms are very similar to those of other illnesses such as colds and flu, which can make them hard to tell apart. The most typical ones are a high temperature, a new continuous cough, and a change in the sense of smell or taste. The NHS also lists shortness of breath, tiredness, body aches and headache, and some people have a sore throat or diarrhoea. It says most people feel better within a few weeks, although recovery can take longer.

The NHS advises staying at home and away from other people when there is a high temperature or a person does not feel well enough to do normal activities. Normal activities can restart once the person feels better or the temperature has gone down. Self-care described by the NHS includes resting, drinking plenty of fluids and considering paracetamol or ibuprofen. For a cough, it suggests avoiding lying flat on the back and not using a fan to cool the room.

sections.heading: Who is at higher risk of becoming seriously ill?
sections.body:
WHO says older adults, people with underlying health conditions and unvaccinated people are at higher risk of severe illness. The conditions it lists include high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, chronic lung, heart, liver and kidney diseases, cancer and dementia. Pregnant women and people with immunosuppression, such as those taking immunosuppressive medicines or living with HIV, are also named as higher-risk groups.

The CDC says the risk of severe illness is greater as the number of underlying conditions increases, and that age is the strongest risk factor. In a US hospital study published by the CDC, pneumonia was the most common respiratory complication among people admitted with COVID-19, and sepsis was also recorded. The NHS offers antiviral medicines to people at highest risk of becoming seriously ill.

sections.heading: How is COVID-19 tested and treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people cannot get free COVID-19 rapid lateral flow tests, though some people at highest risk of serious illness can. Its symptoms page says most people with symptoms do not need to take a rapid lateral flow test. People who are eligible for COVID-19 treatments are advised to take one as soon as symptoms start.

The NHS says home measures such as rest and plenty of fluids can ease symptoms. Antiviral medicines, such as nirmatrelvir with ritonavir (Paxlovid) and molnupiravir (Lagevrio), are offered by the NHS to people at highest risk of becoming seriously ill, and a doctor advises which treatment is most suitable after assessment. The CDC says antiviral treatment has to be started soon after symptoms begin, and advises people at higher risk to talk to a healthcare provider right away, even with mild symptoms. Testing can also help guide treatment decisions, according to the CDC.

sections.heading: How does the vaccination programme work?
sections.body:
The UK runs a seasonal COVID-19 vaccination programme for the groups at highest risk of serious illness. The NHS says the vaccine is available to people aged 75 and over, to people aged 6 months to 74 with a weakened immune system, and to residents of care homes for older adults. For the spring 2026 programme, UKHSA said the groups were the same across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Eligibility for people with a weakened immune system depends on criteria in the Green Book.

The NHS gives examples such as blood cancer, organ, bone marrow or stem cell transplants, HIV and some long-term steroid treatment, and notes that the list does not cover everything. Some people with a severely weakened immune system may need an extra dose. Eligible people can book online or in the NHS App, or go to a walk-in site, without waiting for an invitation. Eligibility has changed between seasons: for autumn and winter 2025/26 it was narrowed to people at highest risk of serious illness.

sections.heading: What is long COVID and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
The NHS describes long COVID, also called post-COVID syndrome, as symptoms of COVID-19 that last longer than 12 weeks. The most common symptoms include extreme tiredness, shortness of breath, joint pain and aching muscles, and problems with memory and concentration. Others include heart palpitations, dizziness, anxiety and depression. Having a mild first illness does not rule it out, as the chance of long-term symptoms does not seem to be linked to how ill someone was at first.

The NHS says there is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms, and physiotherapy for breathing or tiredness is one option. For persistent symptoms the route is a GP appointment; a GP can assess the symptoms, and specialist post-COVID services exist for people whose symptoms have a big impact on their lives. For worsening acute illness, the NHS says to contact a GP or NHS 111 urgently. Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, coughing up blood, or collapsing.

faqs.q: Is COVID-19 the same as flu or a cold?
faqs.a: The NHS says the symptoms of COVID-19 are very similar to those of colds and flu, so they can be hard to tell apart. The most typical COVID-19 symptoms are a high temperature, a new continuous cough and a change in smell or taste. The NHS says most people with symptoms do not need a rapid lateral flow test, but people eligible for COVID-19 treatments are advised to take one as soon as symptoms start.

faqs.q: Who can have the COVID-19 vaccine on the NHS?
faqs.a: The NHS says the vaccine is available to people aged 75 and over, to people aged 6 months to 74 with a weakened immune system, and to residents of care homes for older adults. Its list of conditions and treatments that weaken the immune system does not cover everything, and the full criteria are in the Green Book. Eligible people can book online or in the NHS App, or use a walk-in site. Eligibility can change from one season to the next.

faqs.q: Can COVID-19 be spread by someone with no symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The CDC says anyone infected can spread the virus even without symptoms, and a CDC travel guide says most spread appears to happen early in the infection, particularly in the day or two before symptoms start. WHO says the virus passes through the air in respiratory particles from breathing, talking, coughing or sneezing, and that people are more likely to catch it when close to an infected person or sharing a closed space.

faqs.q: What is long COVID?
faqs.a: Long COVID, also called post-COVID syndrome, is when symptoms of COVID-19 last longer than 12 weeks, according to the NHS. Common symptoms include extreme tiredness, shortness of breath, joint pain, aching muscles and memory and concentration problems. The NHS says there is no cure, but treatment can help manage symptoms. A GP can assess persistent symptoms, and specialist post-COVID services exist for people whose symptoms have a big impact on their lives.

faqs.q: When is COVID-19 an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, coughing up blood, or collapsing. Symptoms that are getting worse or not improving call for urgent contact with a GP or NHS 111, as does a high temperature that lasts five days or more. People at higher risk, such as those who are pregnant, aged 60 or over or have a weakened immune system, are advised to seek advice sooner.

chlamydia.name: Chlamydia
chlamydia.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
chlamydia.overview: Chlamydia is a bacterial infection that is usually spread through sex. The NHS says most people have no symptoms and may not know they have it. When symptoms do occur they can include unusual discharge, pain when passing urine, and pelvic or testicular pain. It can be treated with antibiotics, and WHO describes it as curable. Untreated infection can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and can affect fertility. Testing uses a urine sample or a swab.
causes: Infection with the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
The NHS says it is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex without a condom, or contact with infected genital fluids such as semen or vaginal fluid.
Sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used can also pass it on.
An untreated infection can pass from a pregnant person to the baby during birth.
It is not spread by casual contact such as kissing, hugging or sharing towels or toilet seats.
riskFactors: Sex without a condom.
A new sexual partner, which the NHS lists among the reasons to be tested.
A sexual partner who has been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection.
Being a sexually active woman under 25, the group the English screening programme recommends testing each year.
signs: Unusual vaginal discharge or discharge from the penis.
Bleeding after sex or between periods.
Pain or swelling in the testicles.
Discomfort or discharge from the rectum.
complications: Pelvic inflammatory disease in women, when the infection spreads to the womb, ovaries or fallopian tubes.
Difficulty getting pregnant or infertility, long-lasting pelvic pain and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy after pelvic inflammatory disease.
Pain and swelling of the epididymis in men, which the NHS describes as very rare.
A possible increase in the risk of premature birth or low birthweight when infection is untreated in pregnancy.
Eye infection or pneumonia in a newborn who caught the infection during birth.
chlamydia.diagnosis: Chlamydia is diagnosed by testing a urine sample or a swab. The test most often used is a nucleic acid amplification test, known as a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard. Some areas offer postal home testing kits. Sexual health services advise that testing too soon after possible exposure can miss an infection. In England the national screening programme recommends that sexually active women under 25 are tested each year and after each new partner.
chlamydia.treatment: The NHS says chlamydia can usually be treated effectively with antibiotics, and WHO describes it as curable. The usual antibiotic options are doxycycline and azithromycin tablets. The 2026 BASHH guideline recommends doxycycline as the first-line treatment. Current and recent partners are also tested and treated. The NHS advises avoiding sex until treatment is completed by the person and their partners. Under-25s who have chlamydia are offered another test 3 to 6 months after treatment, to look for reinfection.
chlamydia.prevention: WHO says correct and consistent use of condoms during sex is the most effective way to prevent chlamydia. The CDC, a US source, says condoms and dental dams protect against chlamydia when used correctly every time, including for oral sex. The NHS says sex toys can pass the infection on unless they are washed or covered with a new condom each time. There is no vaccine against chlamydia.
chlamydia.seekCare: A GP, community contraceptive service or sexual health clinic can arrange testing for people with or without symptoms; the NHS lists a new partner or a partner's diagnosis among the reasons to be tested. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 if pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected, and A&E or a call to 999 for severe or worsening pelvic pain, sudden intense lower tummy pain, fainting or feeling very unwell.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of chlamydia?
sections.body:
Most people with chlamydia do not notice any symptoms, according to the NHS, so many do not know they have it. When symptoms do occur, the NHS says they usually appear between 1 and 3 weeks after sex with someone who has chlamydia, though for some people they do not develop until many months later. Symptoms can fade after a few days, but the infection can still be present and can still be passed on.

In women, the NHS lists vaginal discharge that is not normal for the person, bleeding after sex or between periods, a burning feeling when passing urine, and pain in the lower tummy. In men, it lists white, cloudy or watery discharge from the tip of the penis, burning and itching around the penis and testicles, pain and swelling in the testicles, and a burning feeling when passing urine.

Infection of the rectum, which can follow anal sex, can cause discomfort and discharge from the back passage. The CDC notes that chlamydia often causes no symptoms yet can still cause serious harm.

sections.heading: How is chlamydia passed on?
sections.body:
Chlamydia is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. The NHS says it is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex without a condom, and through contact with semen or vaginal fluid, including on sex toys or hands. Sex toys can pass it on if they are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used. The infection can also pass from a pregnant person to the baby during birth.

The NHS says chlamydia is not spread by kissing or hugging, swimming pools, toilet seats, sharing baths or towels, or sharing cups, plates or cutlery.

The NHS lists a new sexual partner, sex without a condom and a partner's diagnosis of a sexually transmitted infection among the situations in which a test is advised.

sections.heading: How is chlamydia diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says the only way to know whether someone has chlamydia is to be tested, and a test can be done whether or not there are symptoms. Testing uses a urine sample or a swab. The NHS says men are usually asked for a urine sample, while women usually take a swab from inside the vagina. Sexual health services advise that testing too soon after possible exposure can miss an infection.

The test most often used is a nucleic acid amplification test, known as a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard for diagnosing the infection. Some areas offer postal home testing kits, particularly for people under 25.

The National Chlamydia Screening Programme in England aims to reduce the harm caused by untreated infection. It recommends that sexually active women under 25 are tested each year and after each new partner.

sections.heading: How is chlamydia treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says chlamydia can usually be treated effectively with antibiotics, and WHO describes it as curable. The usual antibiotic tablets are doxycycline and azithromycin. The 2026 guideline from the British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH) recommends doxycycline as the first-line treatment.

The NHS says current and recent sexual partners should be tested and treated, and that sexual health clinics can help people contact their partners. It advises avoiding sex until the person and their partners have completed treatment, and, after azithromycin, waiting 7 days before sex.

The NHS says under-25s who have chlamydia are offered another test 3 to 6 months after treatment, to look for reinfection. A GP or sexual health clinic can give advice on treatment and follow-up.

sections.heading: What problems can untreated chlamydia cause?
sections.body:
WHO says long-term problems are unlikely if chlamydia is treated early, and that untreated infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and an increased risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy. In women the infection can spread to the womb, ovaries or fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease. The NHS says this can lead to difficulty getting pregnant, long-lasting pelvic pain and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy, and that the risk of problems such as infertility is lower when it is treated early.

In men, the NHS says the infection can spread to the testicles and epididymis, causing pain and swelling, though it describes this as very rare. The NHS says untreated infection could affect fertility in men. In pregnancy, untreated chlamydia may increase the risk of premature birth or low birthweight, and the baby may develop an eye infection or pneumonia after birth.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 if pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected, and A&E or a call to 999 for severe or worsening pelvic pain.

sections.heading: How can chlamydia be prevented?
sections.body:
WHO says correct and consistent use of condoms during sex is the most effective way to prevent chlamydia. The CDC, a US source, says condoms and dental dams protect against chlamydia when used correctly every time, including for oral sex. The NHS says sex toys can pass the infection on unless they are washed or covered with a new condom each time. There is no vaccine against chlamydia, according to WHO.

Because many infections cause no symptoms, testing is how they are found. A sexual health service can arrange testing whether or not there are symptoms. The English screening programme also aims to reduce harm from untreated infection through partner notification and retesting. WHO has a global strategy that aims to reduce new chlamydia cases by 2030.

faqs.q: Can chlamydia be cured?
faqs.a: WHO describes chlamydia as curable, and the NHS says it can usually be treated effectively with antibiotics. Current and recent partners are also tested and treated. The NHS says the risk of problems such as infertility is lower when the infection is treated early. Under-25s who have chlamydia are offered another test 3 to 6 months after treatment, to look for reinfection.

faqs.q: Can you have chlamydia without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says most people with chlamydia do not notice any symptoms and may not know they have it. The CDC says chlamydia often causes no symptoms but can still cause serious harm. The NHS says a test can be done whether or not there are symptoms, and it lists reasons for testing such as a new sexual partner or a partner's diagnosis.

faqs.q: Can chlamydia affect fertility?
faqs.a: Untreated chlamydia can affect fertility. In women, pelvic inflammatory disease can lead to difficulty getting pregnant and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy. The NHS says untreated infection could affect fertility in men. The NHS says the risk of problems such as infertility is lower when the infection is treated early.

faqs.q: How do tests for chlamydia work?
faqs.a: Testing uses a urine sample or a swab. The test most often used is a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard. Some areas offer postal home testing kits. Sexual health services advise that testing too soon after possible exposure can miss an infection, so the timing of a test can matter.

faqs.q: Is chlamydia spread by kissing or sharing towels?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says chlamydia is not spread by kissing, hugging, sharing towels or toilet seats. It is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex without a condom, through contact with infected genital fluids, or by sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time.

faqs.q: What does chlamydia mean for pregnancy?
faqs.a: An untreated infection can pass to the baby during birth. The baby may develop an eye infection or pneumonia. The NHS says untreated chlamydia in pregnancy may also increase the risk of premature birth or low birthweight. The NHS lists pregnancy among the situations in which a test is advised, and a GP or sexual health clinic can arrange one.

kidney-infection.name: Kidney infection (pyelonephritis)
kidney-infection.definition: A kidney infection, also called pyelonephritis, is a urinary tract infection that affects one or both kidneys.
kidney-infection.overview: A kidney infection is a type of urinary tract infection that involves one or both kidneys. The NHS lists pain in the side or lower back, fever and feeling sick among its symptoms, and says it is often caused by cystitis, a bladder infection. It is much more common in women and is also common during pregnancy. If it is not treated it can lead to sepsis, but most people make a full recovery when treatment starts promptly.
causes: Bacteria, often Escherichia coli (E. coli), get into the tube that carries urine out of the body.
Most kidney infections begin as a bladder infection that spreads upwards to the kidneys.
Kidney infection after surgery is rare.
Some infections start in the kidney itself, for example when there is a kidney stone or a kidney abnormality.
riskFactors: Being a woman, because the urethra is shorter.
Pregnancy.
A weakened immune system.
Diabetes.
A kidney stone or a kidney abnormality.
A urinary blockage such as a kidney stone or an enlarged prostate.
A recent bladder infection or repeat kidney infections.
Kidney disease or sickle cell disease.
Vesicoureteral reflux, a urinary tract problem that is more common in children.
Constipation.
signs: Fever and chills.
Pain in the side, lower back or groin.
Dark or cloudy urine, or blood in the urine.
Confusion in older people.
In children younger than 2 years, a high temperature may be the only sign.
complications: Sepsis, which is uncommon but can be life threatening.
Kidney abscess, which clinical reviews list as a complication.
Kidney scarring, which is rare and may progress to chronic kidney disease.
Impaired kidney function or kidney failure.
Preterm labour in pregnancy.
kidney-infection.diagnosis: Clinicians use the history of symptoms, a physical examination and laboratory tests, and may add imaging, according to the NIDDK. A GP can use a dipstick test on a urine sample to show whether a kidney infection is likely. The sample can be sent to a laboratory, which identifies the bacterium and the antibiotics that work against it. Because results can take some days, treatment usually starts straight away. Because kidney infection is much rarer in men, men are routinely investigated further.
kidney-infection.treatment: Antibiotics are the main treatment. The NHS says most people can be treated at home with a course of antibiotics, and possibly painkillers. People with a long-term health condition, or who are pregnant, may need antibiotics through a drip in hospital. NICE guidance gives antibiotics by mouth first when a person can take them and is not severely unwell. The NHS advises paracetamol for pain and a high temperature, and says anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not normally recommended because they may increase the risk of further kidney problems.
kidney-infection.prevention: The NHS says drinking plenty of fluids, mainly water, not holding urine in and wiping from front to back are ways to help prevent urinary tract infections. NHS hospital leaflets add emptying the bladder after sex and treating constipation promptly, because constipation can increase the chance of a bladder or kidney infection. The NIDDK says most kidney infections begin as bladder infections, so bladder infections need prompt treatment, and that experts do not believe diet can prevent or treat kidney infections. For infections that keep coming back, a clinician may prescribe a low-dose antibiotic.
kidney-infection.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E now if there is confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for a very high or very low temperature, pain in the lower tummy or back, blood in the urine, sickness, not having peed all day, or pregnancy with these symptoms. NHS 111 can also be called when a GP cannot be reached or symptoms are getting worse. The NHS says to see a GP when symptoms of a urinary tract infection have not improved after a few days or persist after antibiotics. For a child who may have a kidney infection, the NHS advice is an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a kidney infection?
sections.body:
The NIDDK says kidney infection symptoms usually develop within several hours or over a day. The NIDDK lists fever, chills, and back, side or groin pain among the common signs. The NHS adds tiredness, reduced appetite, feeling or being sick and diarrhoea. Changes in urination, such as burning when peeing, needing to pee more urgently and dark or cloudy urine, can also occur.

Clinical references describe a typical pattern of fever, pain in the flank (the side of the back) and nausea or vomiting, although not every person has all of these. In older people a kidney infection may cause confusion. In children younger than 2 years a kidney infection may cause only a high temperature, and NHS pages say babies may also be irritable and not feed properly.

sections.heading: What causes a kidney infection?
sections.body:
A kidney infection usually happens when bacteria, often a type called E. coli, get into the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body. In most cases the infection starts in the bladder and spreads upwards to the kidneys, and the NHS says it is often caused by cystitis, a bladder infection. The NIDDK says a kidney infection after surgery is rare.

Sometimes a problem in the kidney itself is behind it, such as a kidney stone. A urinary blockage, such as a kidney stone or an enlarged prostate, can raise the risk. Women are affected more often, and the NHS links this to the shorter urethra. The NIDDK says kidney infections are also common during pregnancy. The NHS lists kidney stones, diabetes and a weakened immune system as making infection more likely. The NIDDK adds a recent bladder infection, repeat kidney infections, kidney disease, sickle cell disease and vesicoureteral reflux, a urinary tract problem that is more common in children.

sections.heading: How is a kidney infection diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis combines the story of the symptoms, a physical examination and laboratory tests, according to the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), which says imaging may be added. The NHS says a GP can use a dipstick test on a urine sample to show whether a kidney infection is likely.

The sample can also be sent to a laboratory, where the bacterium is identified and tested against antibiotics. Because the results can take some days, treatment is usually started straight away. Clinical references describe urine culture as central to the diagnosis, and say an ultrasound scan can detect pyelonephritis but a normal scan does not rule it out. Because kidney infection is much rarer in men, the NHS says men are routinely investigated further.

sections.heading: How is a kidney infection treated?
sections.body:
Antibiotics are the main treatment, and the NHS says most people can be treated at home with a course of antibiotics, and possibly painkillers. People with a long-term health condition, or who are pregnant, may need antibiotics through a drip in hospital. In hospital a drip also gives fluids to keep a person hydrated, and treatment usually switches to tablets or capsules afterwards.

NICE guidance on antibiotic prescribing gives antibiotics by mouth first when a person can take them and is not severely unwell. It gives antibiotics into a vein for people who are vomiting, cannot take oral antibiotics or are severely unwell. The NIDDK says incomplete courses of antibiotics can contribute to antibiotic resistance.

The NHS advises paracetamol to reduce a high temperature and relieve pain, and NICE self-care advice includes paracetamol for pain and an adequate intake of fluid. The NHS says anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not normally recommended in a kidney infection because they may increase the risk of further kidney problems.

sections.heading: What are the complications, outlook and ways to prevent it?
sections.body:
The NIDDK says most kidney infections caught early and treated properly do not cause lasting harm. Sepsis is uncommon but can be life threatening, and in rare cases a kidney infection leads to kidney failure or kidney scarring that may progress to chronic kidney disease. NICE lists impaired kidney function, kidney failure, sepsis and preterm labour in pregnancy among the complications of acute pyelonephritis.

Most people make a full recovery when treatment starts promptly. The NHS says it may take up to 2 weeks before someone is fit enough to return to work, and NHS 111 Wales says older people or those with underlying conditions may take longer to recover. The NIDDK says symptoms that come back after treatment need prompt attention from a health care professional.

NHS pages describe drinking plenty of fluids, mainly water, not holding urine in and wiping from front to back as ways to help prevent urinary tract infections. NHS hospital leaflets add emptying the bladder after sex and treating constipation promptly. For people who keep getting urine infections, a clinician may prescribe a low-dose antibiotic.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help?
sections.body:
The NHS lists confusion, drowsiness and difficulty speaking as signs to call 999 or go to A&E now. For a very high or very low temperature, pain in the lower tummy or back, blood in the urine, sickness, not having peed all day, or pregnancy with these symptoms, the NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111.

The NHS says to see a GP when symptoms of a urinary tract infection have not improved after a few days, or when symptoms persist after antibiotics. For a child who may have a kidney infection, the NHS advice is an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111. The NHS says prompt treatment matters because an untreated kidney infection can spread to the bloodstream, and the NIDDK says sepsis, although uncommon, can be life threatening.

faqs.q: Is a kidney infection the same as a urinary tract infection?
faqs.a: A kidney infection is one type of urinary tract infection, the type that affects one or both kidneys. The NHS says it is often caused by cystitis, a bladder infection, and most cases start in the bladder and spread upwards. Its symptoms include pain in the side or lower back and fever, as well as urinary symptoms such as burning when peeing.

faqs.q: Can a kidney infection go away on its own?
faqs.a: The NHS describes antibiotics as the main treatment and says prompt treatment matters, because an untreated infection can spread to the bloodstream. The NIDDK says sepsis, although uncommon, can be life threatening. For symptoms such as a very high or very low temperature, lower tummy or back pain or blood in the urine, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

faqs.q: Why are painkillers like ibuprofen not usually recommended?
faqs.a: The NHS says anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not normally recommended for a kidney infection, because they may increase the risk of further kidney problems. The NHS advises paracetamol to reduce a high temperature and relieve pain, and NICE self-care advice for acute pyelonephritis includes paracetamol for pain and an adequate intake of fluid.

faqs.q: Is a kidney infection more serious in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS lists pregnancy among the reasons to ask for an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 with these symptoms, and says pregnant people may need antibiotics through a drip in hospital. NICE lists preterm labour among the complications of acute pyelonephritis, and says referral or specialist advice should be considered for people aged 16 or over who are pregnant.

faqs.q: How long does it take to recover?
faqs.a: The NHS says most people make a full recovery when treatment starts promptly, and that it may take up to 2 weeks before someone is fit enough to return to work. NHS 111 Wales says older people or those with underlying conditions may take longer to recover. The NIDDK says symptoms that come back after treatment need prompt attention from a health care professional.

tonsillitis.name: Tonsillitis
tonsillitis.definition: An infection of the tonsils, most often caused by a virus and sometimes by bacteria, that brings a sore throat, painful swallowing and fever.
tonsillitis.overview: The tonsils are lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat, one on each side. Tonsillitis is usually caused by a virus, such as the kind behind a cold, though bacteria such as group A streptococcus (strep throat) can also be responsible. It is common in children, teenagers and young adults. The NHS says symptoms usually ease within three to four days, though they can last longer, and NHS sources describe it as usually getting better on its own within a week. Viral cases usually clear up on their own, and a GP may prescribe antibiotics if a bacterial cause is found.
causes: A viral infection, such as a cold or flu virus, is the usual cause
One bacterial cause is group A streptococcus, which also causes strep throat
Most of the infections that lead to tonsillitis, such as colds and flu, are contagious and spread between people
riskFactors: Age: it is most common in children, teenagers and young adults
signs: Swollen, red tonsils
White, pus-filled spots on the tonsils in some people
Swollen, tender glands in the neck
Fever
complications: Quinsy, a pocket of pus between a tonsil and the throat wall, which the NHS describes as a rare but potentially serious complication
Rheumatic fever, which can follow strep throat; MedlinePlus says it does not often occur in the US and other developed countries
Infection that does not improve with antibiotics by mouth and gets worse, for which a GP may refer a person to hospital for antibiotics given into a vein
tonsillitis.diagnosis: A doctor can usually tell that a person has tonsillitis by asking about the symptoms and looking in the throat. A GP may swab the throat to check whether bacteria are the cause; results usually take a few days. A blood test for glandular fever is usually considered when symptoms are severe or persist. For sore throats in general, NICE guidance recommends two scoring tools, FeverPAIN and Centor, to identify people more likely to benefit from an antibiotic.
tonsillitis.treatment: Tonsillitis caused by a virus usually clears up on its own, so treatment is mostly about easing symptoms. The NHS suggests paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, rest, cool drinks and gargling with warm salty water (which it says children should not do), and advises that aspirin is not given to children under 16. A pharmacist can suggest lozenges. If a bacterial cause is found, a GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics by mouth. NICE says antibiotics give only a small benefit for sore throat and that withholding them is unlikely to cause complications, so it recommends a back-up prescription for some people and an immediate prescription for people who are systemically very unwell, have signs of a more serious illness or are at high risk of complications. The NHS says it is very rare for someone to need the tonsils removed (tonsillectomy), and that it is usually only done for severe tonsillitis that keeps coming back.
tonsillitis.prevention: NHS guidance on limiting the spread of colds and flu, which are among the infections that can lead to tonsillitis, suggests washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue and putting it in the bin quickly, and not sharing cups, cutlery or towels.
tonsillitis.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for a severe sore throat that quickly gets worse, swelling inside the mouth or throat, difficulty speaking, swallowing, breathing or opening the mouth, which can be signs of quinsy. The NHS says to get help from NHS 111 now for pus-filled spots on the tonsils or a sore throat so painful that eating or drinking is difficult. A GP appointment is advised when symptoms have not gone away within about a week, or when throat infections keep coming back; NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if symptoms last longer than four days without improving, and NHS 111 can advise when the surgery is closed. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not start to improve after a week, or the person becomes very unwell.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of tonsillitis?
sections.body:
The usual symptoms of tonsillitis are a sore throat, pain when swallowing, earache and fever. The tonsils may look swollen and red, and some people have white, pus-filled spots on them. The glands in the neck can become swollen and tender.

The NHS says symptoms usually ease within three to four days, although they can last longer. NHS sources describe tonsillitis as an illness that usually gets better on its own within a week. Tonsillitis is common in children, teenagers and young adults.

When symptoms do not go away, the advice differs slightly by source. The NHS page advises a GP appointment if symptoms have not gone away within a week, while NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if symptoms last longer than four days without showing signs of getting better. NHS inform adds that NHS 111 can advise when the surgery is closed.

sections.heading: What causes tonsillitis?
sections.body:
Most cases of tonsillitis are caused by a virus, such as the kind behind a cold. Bacteria can also be responsible. One bacterial cause is group A streptococcus, which also causes strep throat.

The NHS says tonsillitis itself is not contagious, but the infections that cause it, for example colds and flu, are. Tonsillitis is common in children, teenagers and young adults.

Telling a viral from a bacterial cause matters because treatment differs. Viral tonsillitis usually clears up on its own, while a GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics by mouth if a bacterial cause is found. NICE says antibiotics give only a small benefit for sore throat and that withholding them is unlikely to cause complications. Quinsy, a pocket of pus beside a tonsil, usually develops after a bacterial infection spreads from the tonsil.

sections.heading: How is tonsillitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
A doctor can usually tell that a person has tonsillitis by asking about the symptoms and looking in the throat. A GP may swab the throat to check whether bacteria are the cause, and results usually take a few days. A blood test for glandular fever is usually considered when symptoms are severe or persist.

For sore throats in general, NICE recommends that clinicians use one of two scoring tools, FeverPAIN or Centor, to identify the people more likely to benefit from an antibiotic. People with low scores are unlikely to benefit and are given self-care advice rather than an antibiotic. For higher scores the clinician considers an immediate or a back-up prescription, which is handed over with advice not to start it straight away and to use it only if there is no improvement. NICE notes that its committee said the scoring tools have not been validated in a UK population.

Difficulty breathing is an emergency, and the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

sections.heading: How is tonsillitis treated?
sections.body:
Because viral tonsillitis usually clears up on its own, treatment is mostly about easing symptoms. The NHS suggests paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, rest, cool drinks and gargling with warm salty water, which it says children should not do. NICE lists paracetamol for pain or fever, with ibuprofen as an alternative if preferred and suitable, and advises an adequate intake of fluids. The NHS advises that aspirin is not given to children under 16. A pharmacist can suggest lozenges, and NHS sources say gargles and sprays may soothe a sore throat but do not shorten the illness.

A GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics by mouth if a bacterial cause is found. NICE says that for people who are systemically very unwell, have symptoms and signs of a more serious illness, or are at high risk of complications, an immediate antibiotic prescription should be offered. If antibiotics by mouth do not help and symptoms are getting worse, a GP may refer a person to hospital for antibiotics given into a vein.

sections.heading: What are the complications of tonsillitis?
sections.body:
Complications of tonsillitis are rare. The best known is quinsy, also called a peritonsillar abscess, in which a pocket of pus builds up between a tonsil and the wall of the throat, usually after a bacterial infection spreads from the tonsil. The NHS describes it as a rare but potentially serious complication. Quinsy can happen at any age but is most common in teenagers and young adults, and it can come back.

The NHS lists the signs that can point to quinsy as a severe sore throat that quickly gets worse, swelling inside the mouth or throat, and difficulty speaking, swallowing, breathing or opening the mouth. For these signs the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

Rheumatic fever is another possible complication of strep throat. MedlinePlus, a US source, says it does not often occur in the United States and other developed countries.

sections.heading: When is tonsil removal considered?
sections.body:
Removal of the tonsils is called a tonsillectomy. The NHS says it is very rare for someone to need it, and that it is usually only done for severe tonsillitis that keeps coming back. Eligibility criteria vary by area. Scottish referral guidance, used by several NHS areas, says the sore throats should be due to acute tonsillitis and disabling enough to prevent normal functioning, and it sets thresholds for how many episodes there have been over one or more years. If a person does not meet them, it advises a period of watchful waiting with a symptom diary.

Leaflets from NHS hospital trusts describe the operation as done under general anaesthetic, with the tonsils taken out through the mouth, so there is no cut on the outside of the neck. They describe a sore throat that can last about two weeks, with some saying up to three weeks, and earache is common. Bleeding can happen up to about two weeks afterwards. The leaflets advise going to A&E for fresh bleeding or coughing up or vomiting blood, and calling 999 if bleeding is heavy or will not stop. Trusts' advice differs, so the leaflet from the hospital involved applies.

faqs.q: Is tonsillitis contagious?
faqs.a: The NHS says tonsillitis itself is not contagious, but the infections that cause it, such as colds and flu, are. NHS guidance on limiting the spread of colds and flu includes washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue and binning it quickly, and not sharing cups, cutlery or towels.

faqs.q: How long does tonsillitis last?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms usually ease within three to four days but can last longer. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not start to improve after a week, or the person becomes very unwell. NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if symptoms last longer than four days without improving.

faqs.q: Are antibiotics needed for tonsillitis?
faqs.a: Viral tonsillitis usually clears up on its own. A GP may prescribe antibiotics when bacteria are the cause. NICE says antibiotics give only a small benefit for sore throat, and that scoring tools help decide between self-care advice, a back-up prescription or an immediate prescription for people who are very unwell or at high risk of complications.

faqs.q: When does tonsillitis need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for a severe sore throat that quickly gets worse, swelling inside the mouth or throat, or difficulty speaking, swallowing, breathing or opening the mouth, which can be signs of quinsy. NHS 111 is the route for pus-filled spots on the tonsils or a sore throat so painful that eating or drinking is difficult. A GP appointment is advised if symptoms have not gone within about a week.

faqs.q: Is tonsil removal the usual treatment?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says it is very rare for someone to need their tonsils removed, and that it is usually only done for severe tonsillitis that keeps coming back. Eligibility criteria vary by area, and Scottish referral guidance advises a period of watchful waiting with a symptom diary for people who do not meet the criteria.

ear-infection.name: Ear infection (otitis media)
ear-infection.definition: An ear infection is an infection, usually of the middle ear behind the eardrum, that is common in children and often settles without treatment.
ear-infection.overview: Ear infections are common, especially in children, and usually settle without intervention. In the middle ear, blocked or swollen eustachian tubes let fluid build up behind the eardrum, which can lead to infection. Both viruses and bacteria can be responsible. Typical signs are earache, a fever, difficulty hearing and fluid leaking from the ear. Many ear infections get better on their own within about 3 days, and complications are rare.
causes: Both viruses and bacteria can cause ear infections.
The CDC names Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae as the two most common bacteria involved.
When the eustachian tube is blocked, fluid can collect behind the eardrum and become infected.
MedlinePlus lists allergies, colds and sinus infections, teething, enlarged adenoids and tobacco smoke as contributing factors.
riskFactors: Attending daycare
Using a pacifier
Not being breastfed
A family history of ear infections
Exposure to tobacco smoke: the CDC says children whose parents smoke around them get more ear infections
Young age: ear infections are common, especially in children
signs: Redness of the eardrum, a bulging eardrum or fluid behind it on looking into the ear
Discharge from the ear, which can come through a perforated eardrum
Fluid in the middle ear detected by pneumatic otoscopy
complications: Slight short-term hearing loss during and just after the infection, because of fluid in the ear
Glue ear, a build-up of fluid in the middle ear that can follow colds and infections
A torn (perforated) eardrum, which is rare
Spread of infection to the mastoid bone behind the ear (mastoiditis) or, rarely, to the meninges
Chronic otitis media or an abscess, which are rare
ear-infection.diagnosis: A clinician usually looks into the ear with an otoscope, checking for redness, a bulging eardrum or fluid behind it. Pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry are used to confirm fluid in the middle ear. If a child's hearing is a worry, a GP can refer them to audiology for a hearing test.
ear-infection.treatment: Many cases get better on their own, and for mild cases a clinician may recommend watchful waiting or delayed antibiotic prescribing. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort. Antibiotics are not usually offered for middle ear infections, because they make little difference to symptoms. NICE guideline NG91 describes no antibiotic or a back-up antibiotic prescription as the options for most children with acute otitis media, with some exceptions. A GP or pharmacist may prescribe eardrops or tablets for some types of ear infection.
ear-infection.prevention: The CDC advises receiving recommended vaccines, such as the flu and pneumococcal vaccines, because pneumococcal vaccine protects against a common cause of middle ear infections. The CDC also advises not smoking and avoiding secondhand smoke. MedlinePlus lists hand washing, breastfeeding and avoiding pacifiers among ways to lower risk.
ear-infection.seekCare: The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 if the person feels generally unwell, has a very high temperature, swelling around the ear, new hearing loss, fluid coming out of the ear, dizziness or vomiting. A child under 12 months with earache in both ears is also on that list. The NHS advises seeing a GP if earache lasts more than 3 days or keeps coming back. One NHS trust page says to call 999 or go to an urgent and emergency care centre for extreme pain, or for pain, tenderness, swelling or redness over the bone behind the ear. In an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of an ear infection?
sections.body:
The main signs of an ear infection are earache, a fever, difficulty hearing and fluid leaking from the ear. The NHS describes ear infections as common, especially in children. Young children and babies may rub or pull at the ear, be irritable or restless, be off their food, not react to some sounds or keep losing their balance. MedlinePlus says infants may show mainly irritability or crying that is hard to soothe, while older children and adults more often report ear pain, a feeling of fullness and hearing loss in the affected ear.

The NHS says that ear infections often get better on their own within about 3 days, although symptoms can sometimes last up to a week. The CDC lists symptoms lasting more than 2 to 3 days, worsening symptoms, and pus or fluid draining from the ear as reasons to see a healthcare provider. Discharge from the ear can come through a perforated eardrum.

sections.heading: What causes ear infections?
sections.body:
Both viruses and bacteria can cause an ear infection. The CDC names Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae as the two most common bacteria involved, and says cold viruses can also cause middle ear infections. The eustachian tube normally drains fluid from the middle ear. When it becomes blocked, fluid can collect behind the eardrum and become infected. MedlinePlus lists allergies, colds and sinus infections, excess mucus and saliva during teething, infected or overgrown adenoids and tobacco smoke as contributing factors.

Several risk factors are described. A 2017 review found that day care attendance and a family history of ear infections remain major risk factors. MedlinePlus lists pacifier use among the risk factors, and one Australian study linked not being breastfed with ear infection. The CDC says children whose parents smoke around them get more ear infections. The CDC also says pneumococcal vaccine protects against a common cause of middle ear infections.

sections.heading: How is an ear infection diagnosed?
sections.body:
A clinician usually looks into the ear with an otoscope. They check for redness, a bulging eardrum or fluid behind the eardrum. Reviews list fever, discharge from the ear, a full or bulging cloudy eardrum, reduced movement of the eardrum and redness as signs of acute otitis media. Ear pain is one of the more reliable indicators, but many young children show only nonspecific signs.

Pneumatic otoscopy and tympanometry are used to confirm fluid in the middle ear. One review notes that a diagnosis of acute otitis media should not be made when these tests do not show fluid. Infection of the outer ear, known as swimmer's ear, is a separate condition from a middle ear infection. If a child's hearing is a worry, a GP can refer them to audiology for a hearing test.

sections.heading: How is an ear infection treated?
sections.body:
Many cases get better on their own, so a clinician may recommend watchful waiting. The CDC says a provider may suggest waiting 2 to 3 days before prescribing antibiotics for a mild infection. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort, and the NHS says children under 16 should not take aspirin. The NHS advises keeping cotton buds and fingers out of the ear, keeping water out of it and not swimming during an ear infection. Decongestants and antihistamines are not recommended, because there is no evidence that they help.

NICE says most ear infections clear up within 3 days, although symptoms can sometimes last up to a week. Antibiotics are not usually offered for middle ear infections, because they make little difference to symptoms. NICE guideline NG91 describes no antibiotic or a back-up antibiotic prescription as the options for most children. A back-up prescription can be used if symptoms significantly worsen or do not improve within 3 days. Immediate antibiotics are offered where a child is very unwell, has signs of a more serious illness or is at high risk of complications. NICE says antibiotics might also be given if fluid is coming out of the ear, or if a child under 2 has infection in both ears.

sections.heading: What complications can an ear infection cause?
sections.body:
Most children have slight short-term hearing loss during and just after an ear infection, because of fluid in the ear. MedlinePlus lists rarer complications as a torn eardrum, spread of infection to the mastoid bone behind the ear or to the meninges, chronic otitis media and abscess. Swelling and tenderness behind the ear are among the signs of mastoiditis described in reviews.

Glue ear is a build-up of fluid in the middle ear. The NHS says it often clears up on its own within 3 months. Hospital leaflets describe it as especially common in young children, most often between 2 and 5, with mild to moderate hearing loss that may affect one or both ears. One UK parent guide says glue ear needs treating only if it causes persistent hearing loss, speech delay or recurrent ear infections. Grommets are tiny tubes placed in the eardrum, and hearing aids are another option for persistent glue ear. The NHS says antibiotics are not a standard treatment for glue ear.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help?
sections.body:
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 if a person with ear infection symptoms feels generally unwell, has a very high temperature, has swelling around the ear, has new hearing loss, has fluid coming out of the ear, or feels dizzy or is being sick. A child under 12 months with earache in both ears is also on that list.

The NHS advises seeing a GP if earache lasts more than 3 days or keeps coming back. One NHS trust page says to call 999 or go to an urgent and emergency care centre for extreme pain, or for pain, tenderness, swelling or redness over the bone behind the ear. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists swelling behind the ear, severe pain, a high fever, severe headache, dizziness and twitching of the facial muscles as reasons to contact a health care provider. In an emergency, call 999.

faqs.q: Do ear infections go away on their own?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The NHS says most ear infections get better by themselves, usually within about 3 days, although symptoms can sometimes last up to a week. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort in the meantime. The NHS advises seeing a GP if earache lasts more than 3 days, and NHS 111 or an urgent GP appointment if the person feels generally unwell or fluid comes out of the ear.

faqs.q: Do ear infections need antibiotics?
faqs.a: Usually not. The NHS says antibiotics are not usually offered for middle ear infections because they make little difference to symptoms. NICE describes no antibiotic or a back-up prescription as the options for most children with acute otitis media. Immediate antibiotics are offered where a child is very unwell, has signs of a more serious illness or is at high risk of complications.

faqs.q: Is an ear infection the same as glue ear?
faqs.a: Not quite. Glue ear is a build-up of fluid in the middle ear, and colds, infections, allergies and enlarged adenoids can all block the eustachian tube. The NHS says antibiotics may be prescribed if glue ear causes an ear infection, but they are not a standard treatment for glue ear itself. Hospital leaflets describe the hearing loss as usually mild or moderate.

faqs.q: Can ear infections be prevented?
faqs.a: The CDC advises receiving recommended vaccines, such as the flu and pneumococcal vaccines, because pneumococcal vaccine protects against a common cause of middle ear infections. The CDC also advises not smoking and avoiding secondhand smoke. MedlinePlus lists hand washing, breastfeeding and avoiding pacifiers among ways to lower risk.

faqs.q: Can an ear infection affect hearing?
faqs.a: Most children have slight short-term hearing loss during and just after an ear infection, because of fluid in the ear. Glue ear, a build-up of fluid in the middle ear, can also cause mild to moderate hearing loss. New hearing loss is on the NHS list of reasons to ask for an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

thrush.name: Thrush (candidiasis)
thrush.definition: A common yeast infection caused by Candida, a fungus that normally lives harmlessly on the body, which can affect the mouth, the genitals and the skin.
thrush.overview: Thrush is an infection caused by Candida, which lives on the skin and in places such as the mouth, throat and vagina, usually without causing symptoms. It can cause problems in the genital area of women and men, in the mouth, and on areas of skin such as the armpits and groin. The NHS says it is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, although it can be triggered by sex or, less often, passed on during sex. It is usually treated with antifungal medicine.
causes: Thrush is caused by Candida, a fungus that is normally harmless.
In the vagina, normal bacteria usually keep the growth of the yeast under control.
Sex can trigger genital thrush, and less often it is passed on during sex.
The CDC gives a weakened immune system and antibiotic use as general risks for candidiasis.
riskFactors: Taking antibiotics
Poorly controlled diabetes
A weakened immune system, for example from HIV or chemotherapy
Pregnancy and hormone replacement therapy
Irritated or damaged skin
For oral thrush: steroid inhalers, including some asthma inhalers, dentures and antibiotics
For oral thrush: dry mouth and poor oral hygiene
Being a baby under one month old, or living with HIV/AIDS, for infection of the mouth, throat or oesophagus
signs: A white, often odourless discharge with itching and irritation around the vagina and vulva
Redness and irritation around the head of the penis and under the foreskin, sometimes with a white discharge
Red areas with white patches in the mouth of an adult with oral thrush
A white coating on the tongue in babies
A red, itchy rash in skin folds such as the armpits, groin and under the breasts
complications: Thrush that keeps coming back, which may need longer treatment
Painful or difficult swallowing when the throat or oesophagus is involved
Passing thrush back and forth between a breastfeeding mother and her baby
Invasive candidiasis, which can involve the bloodstream and is a separate condition; the CDC says most people are not at risk of it
thrush.diagnosis: UK sexual health guidance (BASHH) says the diagnosis of candidiasis rests on symptoms and clinical findings together, not on culture results alone. If it is unclear, the area may be examined and a cotton bud used on the discharge to test for other infections. If thrush keeps coming back, a vaginal swab may be taken to check whether a different kind of yeast is the cause. For men, a GP will want to confirm that it is thrush and rule out other infections. The BASHH guideline on recurrent vulvovaginal thrush expects diagnosis to be confirmed by microscopy or culture when symptoms are present.
thrush.treatment: Thrush is usually treated with antifungal medicine, given as a tablet, a pessary placed in the vagina, or a cream. The NHS says thrush in men and women should clear up within 7 to 14 days of starting treatment. Partners generally do not need treatment unless they have symptoms. Treatment may be given for longer if thrush keeps coming back. For oral thrush, a pharmacist can supply an antifungal mouth gel. When a breastfeeding mother and her baby have thrush, both are treated at the same time. For skin thrush, MedlinePlus says antifungal skin creams, ointments or powders may be used.
thrush.prevention: The NHS suggests washing the genital area with water or an emollient instead of soap, drying thoroughly, wearing cotton underwear, and avoiding douching. For oral thrush, the NHS lists good dental care, rinsing the mouth after using inhalers, not wearing dentures at night and not smoking.
thrush.seekCare: A GP appointment, or a sexual health clinic, is the route the NHS suggests for a first episode of symptoms, treatment that has not worked, or thrush that keeps returning. Treatments can be bought from a pharmacy, and a pharmacist can recommend one. Pregnancy, breastfeeding and a weakened immune system are also reasons to get advice. For oral thrush, the NHS lists these reasons for a non-urgent GP appointment: no improvement after a week of mouth gel, difficult or painful swallowing, a baby under 4 months with signs of thrush, or a weakened immune system.

sections.heading: What is thrush?
sections.body:
Thrush is an infection caused by Candida, a fungus that is normally harmless. The CDC says Candida is normally present on the body and that most of the time it causes no symptoms. The CDC lists several types of candidiasis, including vaginal yeast infections, oral thrush and skin infections. The NHS says thrush can affect the genital area in both men and women, and can also appear on other areas of skin such as the armpits, groin and between the fingers.

Oral thrush, also called mouth thrush, is described by the NHS as usually harmless and common in babies and in older people with dentures. Oral thrush in adults is not contagious, according to the NHS. Thrush is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, but it can be triggered by sex or, less often, passed on during sex.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of thrush?
sections.body:
In women, the NHS lists a white discharge that is often odourless and may look like cottage cheese, with itching and irritation around the vagina and vulva. Stinging during sex or when passing urine can also occur. In men, symptoms can include irritation, burning and redness around the head of the penis and under the foreskin, a white discharge, an unpleasant smell, and difficulty pulling back the foreskin.

In oral thrush, adults may have a red mouth with white patches, while babies may have a white coating on the tongue. The CDC adds that infection of the oesophagus can cause pain and difficulty swallowing. On the skin, MedlinePlus describes intense itching with rashes in skin folds, the genitals and under the breasts. The CDC describes skin infection as an itching or burning rash with skin breakdown.

sections.heading: What causes thrush and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
Candida is normally harmless, and in the vagina normal bacteria usually keep its growth under control. The NHS lists several things that raise the risk, including antibiotics, poorly controlled diabetes, a weakened immune system, hormone replacement therapy and pregnancy. Irritated or damaged skin is also mentioned. The CDC says pregnancy and hormone changes raise the risk of vaginal candidiasis.

For oral thrush, NHS inform lists recent antibiotics, inhaled steroids such as some asthma inhalers, dentures, poor oral hygiene and dry mouth. The CDC says babies under one month old and people with HIV/AIDS have a higher risk of candidiasis in the mouth, throat or oesophagus. Diabetes UK says high sugar in the urine raises the risk of thrush, which is one reason diabetes is linked with it. NHS inform says that, for oral thrush, a GP may sometimes recommend blood tests to check for conditions such as diabetes.

sections.heading: How is thrush diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
UK sexual health guidance (BASHH) says the diagnosis of candidiasis rests on symptoms and clinical findings together, not on culture results alone. If it is unclear, the area may be examined and a cotton bud used on the discharge to test for other infections. If thrush keeps coming back, a vaginal swab may be taken to check whether a different kind of yeast is the cause. For men, the NHS says a GP will want to confirm that it is thrush and rule out other infections. The BASHH guideline on recurrent vulvovaginal thrush expects diagnosis to be confirmed by microscopy or culture when symptoms are present.

Treatment is usually an antifungal medicine, given as a tablet, a pessary placed in the vagina, or a cream to ease irritation. The NHS says thrush in men and women should clear up within 7 to 14 days of starting treatment, and that partners generally do not need treatment unless they have symptoms. If thrush keeps coming back, treatment may be given for longer. For oral thrush, a pharmacist can supply an antifungal mouth gel.

sections.heading: Thrush in pregnancy, babies and breastfeeding
sections.body:
The CDC says pregnancy and hormone changes raise the risk of vaginal candidiasis, and the NHS says there is no evidence that thrush can harm an unborn baby. The NHS advises pregnant women to check with a GP or midwife before using any thrush treatment. The NHS advises against anti-thrush tablets in pregnancy, when trying to conceive or while breastfeeding, and describes a cream or pessary as the alternative. A baby can also catch thrush during delivery if the mother has it.

About 1 in 7 babies develops oral thrush at some point, according to a Kingston and Richmond NHS Foundation Trust leaflet. White patches on a baby's tongue that do not rub off easily can point to thrush, whereas a milk coating usually rubs off. If a breastfeeding mother or her baby has thrush, both are treated at the same time because it can easily spread between them. Breastfeeding can continue during treatment.

sections.heading: How can thrush be prevented, and when should medical help be sought?
sections.body:
The NHS suggests washing the genital area with water or an emollient instead of soap, drying thoroughly, wearing cotton underwear, and avoiding douching. For oral thrush, it lists good dental care, rinsing the mouth after using inhalers, not wearing dentures at night and not smoking.

A GP appointment, or a sexual health clinic, is the route the NHS suggests for a first episode, treatment that has not worked or thrush that keeps returning. Pregnancy, breastfeeding and a weakened immune system are also reasons to get advice, and a pharmacist can advise on treatment. For oral thrush, non-urgent GP advice is suggested if there is no improvement after a week of mouth gel, if swallowing is difficult or painful, or if a baby under 4 months has signs of thrush. The CDC separately describes invasive candidiasis, which can involve the bloodstream, and says most people are not at risk of it.

faqs.q: Is thrush a sexually transmitted infection?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says thrush is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, although sex can trigger it and, less often, it can be passed on during sex. Partners generally do not need treatment unless they have symptoms. A GP or sexual health clinic can confirm the cause and rule out other infections.

faqs.q: How long does thrush take to clear?
faqs.a: The NHS says thrush in men and women should clear up within 7 to 14 days of starting treatment. If treatment has not worked, or thrush keeps coming back, the NHS suggests seeing a GP. A swab may be taken to check the cause, and treatment may be given for longer.

faqs.q: Can men get thrush?
faqs.a: Yes. In men the NHS describes irritation, burning and redness around the head of the penis and under the foreskin, sometimes with a white discharge, an unpleasant smell or difficulty pulling back the foreskin. A GP will want to confirm that it is thrush and rule out other infections.

faqs.q: Is oral thrush contagious?
faqs.a: The NHS says oral thrush in adults is not contagious. In breastfeeding, thrush can easily spread between a mother and her baby, so both are treated at the same time. The NHS describes oral thrush as usually harmless and common in babies and older people with dentures.

faqs.q: Can thrush affect the skin?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says thrush can affect other areas of skin, such as the armpits, groin and between the fingers. MedlinePlus describes intense itching with rashes in skin folds, the genitals and under the breasts. MedlinePlus says antifungal skin creams, ointments or powders may be used to treat a yeast infection of the skin.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.definition: Meningitis is an infection of the protective membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.
meningitis.overview: The NHS says meningitis is usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection, and fungi can also be a cause. Viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious, while bacterial meningitis is the more serious form and needs treatment in hospital. Symptoms can develop suddenly. The NHS gives the same emergency advice for meningitis and sepsis: call 999 or go to A&E. Vaccination is the main way of preventing some causes of meningitis.
causes: A viral or bacterial infection is the usual cause.
Fungi can also cause meningitis, and fungal cases often develop slowly.
Viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious.
Bacterial meningitis is the more serious form.
The infections spread mainly through very close contact with a person carrying the infection.
riskFactors: Prolonged close contact with a person who has meningococcal disease in a household-type setting in the 7 days before their illness began.
UKHSA also counts intimate kissing or equivalent close contact, and exposure to respiratory secretions, as close contact with a case.
signs: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is a key warning sign, though not everyone with meningitis has one.
A stiff neck.
In babies, a bulging soft spot on the top of the head.
Cold hands and feet and fast breathing can occur when bacteria enter the bloodstream and cause sepsis.
Bacterial meningitis may be missed in older adults who have delirium or altered consciousness.
complications: Hearing loss or vision loss.
Seizures.
Problems with movement, balance and coordination.
Difficulty with memory and concentration.
Loss of digits or limbs in some people.
Sepsis.
meningitis.diagnosis: The doctor examines the person, asks about symptoms and may arrange blood tests and a lumbar puncture, which collects a sample of cerebrospinal fluid for examination. A CT scan may be used to look for brain problems such as swelling. When bacterial infection is suspected, antibiotics usually start before the diagnosis is confirmed, and the WHO says a lumbar puncture should never delay them.
meningitis.treatment: Treatment depends on whether the cause is viral or bacterial. Bacterial meningitis is treated in hospital, usually for at least a week, with antibiotics and fluids given into a vein and oxygen through a face mask if needed. Steroid medicine may be given in some cases to reduce swelling around the brain. Viral meningitis usually improves on its own within 7 to 10 days and can often be managed at home with rest, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine. Fungal meningitis is treated with antifungal medicine.
meningitis.prevention: The NHS describes vaccination as the main way to prevent some causes of meningitis, with MenB for babies, MenACWY for teenagers and the 6-in-1, pneumococcal and MMRV vaccines. Close contacts of someone with meningococcal disease are offered preventive antibiotics.
meningitis.seekCare: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to the nearest A&E immediately if meningitis or sepsis is suspected, and notes that a rash does not always develop. NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear whether symptoms are serious. UKHSA guidance says close contacts who become unwell should seek medical advice.
