sections.heading: What are the symptoms of meningitis?
sections.body:
The NHS says meningitis symptoms can develop suddenly. They include a high temperature, very cold hands and feet, a stiff neck, joint and muscle pain, and a severe headache that keeps getting worse. NHS pages note that early symptoms can resemble flu, a stomach bug or a hangover. A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is a key warning sign, but a rash does not always develop. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E immediately if meningitis or sepsis is suspected.

Babies and young children can show different signs, such as refusing feeds, a high-pitched cry or a bulging soft spot on the top of the head. The WHO adds that infants often have different symptoms from adults, including unusual drowsiness or inactivity and irritability.

The NICE guideline says a non-blanching rash is mainly associated with meningococcal disease, and that bacterial meningitis should not be ruled out just because a person lacks some of the listed signs. It notes that bacterial meningitis may be missed in older adults with delirium or altered consciousness, and that fever is less common in older adults.

sections.heading: What causes meningitis and how does it spread?
sections.body:
The NHS says meningitis is usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection. Viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious, while bacterial meningitis is the more serious form. Meningitis Now says fungal meningitis often develops slowly, with vague symptoms such as tiredness and a persistent headache, and the CDC says it typically affects only people with weakened immune systems.

The NHS says the infections that cause meningitis spread mainly through very close contact with a person carrying the infection, even if they have no symptoms. UKHSA guidance on meningococcal disease counts prolonged close contact with the case in a household-type setting during the 7 days before the illness began, intimate kissing or equivalent close contact, and exposure to respiratory secretions. It says sharing a water bottle or toys that may be mouthed is not considered a high-risk way of spreading meningococcal disease.

The WHO notes that some bacteria can enter the bloodstream and quickly cause sepsis, with signs such as cold hands and feet, fast breathing and low blood pressure. It adds that a non-blanching skin rash may appear with meningococcal sepsis.

sections.heading: How is meningitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
NHS material says the doctor examines the person, asks about symptoms and may arrange blood tests and a lumbar puncture. A lumbar puncture collects a sample of cerebrospinal fluid so that it can be examined. A CT scan may be used to look for problems such as swelling.

When a bacterial cause is suspected, NHS material says antibiotics usually start before the diagnosis is confirmed and are stopped later if tests show that a virus is the cause. The WHO says a lumbar puncture should be done before antibiotics where possible, but that when bacterial meningitis is suspected from the signs and symptoms, it should never delay antibiotic treatment.

For people with suspected bacterial meningitis, NICE recommends a bacterial throat swab for meningococcal culture, preferably taken before antibiotics are started. NICE also says blood tests should be taken before antibiotics, and describes taking blood samples, giving antibiotics and stabilising the person before imaging.

sections.heading: How is meningitis treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on whether the cause is viral or bacterial. The NHS says bacterial meningitis needs treatment in hospital, usually for at least a week. Hospital care includes antibiotics and fluids given directly into a vein, and oxygen through a face mask if needed. Steroid medicine may be given in some cases to reduce swelling around the brain, and the WHO recommends corticosteroids with the first antibiotic dose in non-epidemic settings.

NICE says a senior clinical decision maker should make sure antibiotics for suspected meningococcal disease start within 1 hour of the person arriving at hospital. It also says transfer to hospital should not be delayed to give antibiotics, and that for strongly suspected meningococcal disease an antibiotic should be given as soon as possible outside hospital unless there is a severe allergy. UKHSA guidance gives rapid admission to hospital as the highest priority when invasive meningococcal disease is suspected.

The NHS says viral meningitis tends to get better on its own within 7 to 10 days. It can often be treated at home with rest, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine. The CDC says fungal meningitis is treated with antifungal medicines.

sections.heading: Can meningitis be prevented?
sections.body:
The NHS says several vaccines offer some protection against meningitis, because it can be caused by a number of different infections. NHS vaccination pages list MenB for babies, MenACWY for teenagers in school year 9 (with a catch-up up to age 25 if missed), and the 6-in-1, pneumococcal and MMRV vaccines. The WHO says vaccines offer the best protection against common types of bacterial meningitis, but that no universal vaccine exists. The NHS adds that MenACWY does not prevent all types, so knowing the symptoms still matters after vaccination.

UKHSA guidance says close contacts of someone with meningococcal disease are offered preventive antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of the first person's diagnosis, regardless of vaccination status. It says close contacts can attend education and early years settings as normal, and does not advise face masks in those settings to prevent spread.

The guidance adds that contacts who become unwell should seek medical advice. In an emergency the NHS route is 999 or A&E.

sections.heading: What are the after-effects and how does recovery go?
sections.body:
The after-effects of meningitis depend on the cause. Meningitis Now says long-term after-effects of viral meningitis can include headaches, exhaustion and memory loss.

The NHS says bacterial meningitis can cause long-term problems such as hearing or vision loss, seizures, problems with movement and coordination, and problems with memory and concentration. Meningitis Now says amputation of fingers, toes or limbs may be necessary in severe meningococcal septicaemia. The WHO says about one in five people who survive bacterial meningitis may have long-lasting after-effects. Meningitis Research Foundation says most children who have bacterial meningitis or meningococcal sepsis survive without permanent after-effects, while a Great Ormond Street Hospital press release reported that one in three children who had meningococcal group B disease were left with after-effects.

The NHS says prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation support may help if limbs were amputated, and that counselling and psychological support may help if the experience causes problems such as disturbed sleep or fear of doctors and hospitals. Meningitis Research Foundation and Meningitis Now offer information and support.

faqs.q: How are meningitis and sepsis linked?
faqs.a: The NHS gives the same emergency advice for both: call 999 or go to A&E immediately if either is suspected. The WHO notes that some bacteria that cause meningitis can enter the bloodstream and quickly cause sepsis, with signs such as cold hands and feet, fast breathing and low blood pressure, and that a non-blanching rash may appear with meningococcal sepsis.

faqs.q: What is the difference between viral and bacterial meningitis?
faqs.a: The NHS says viral meningitis is the most common type and the least serious, while bacterial meningitis is more serious. Bacterial meningitis needs hospital treatment, usually for at least a week, with antibiotics into a vein. Viral meningitis usually improves on its own within 7 to 10 days and can often be managed at home.

faqs.q: Does everyone with meningitis get a rash?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is a key warning sign, but a rash does not always develop. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E immediately if meningitis or sepsis is suspected, and NHS pages say a non-fading rash can be a sign of sepsis that needs a 999 call straight away.

faqs.q: Is meningitis contagious?
faqs.a: The NHS says the infections that cause meningitis spread mainly through very close contact with a person carrying the infection. UKHSA says close contacts of a person with meningococcal disease are offered preventive antibiotics, can attend education settings as normal, and should seek medical advice if they become unwell.

faqs.q: What are the long-term effects of meningitis?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. Meningitis Now says viral meningitis can have long-term after-effects such as headaches, exhaustion and memory loss. The NHS says bacterial meningitis can cause hearing loss, vision loss, seizures or memory and concentration problems. Meningitis Research Foundation says most children who have bacterial meningitis or meningococcal sepsis survive without permanent after-effects.

hiv.name: HIV
hiv.definition: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system and, with treatment, can be managed as a long-term condition.
hiv.overview: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system. The NHS says most people have a short flu-like illness 2 to 6 weeks after infection, and the virus may then cause no further symptoms for many years. HIV is not the same as AIDS, which is the most advanced stage of infection. There is currently no cure, but the NHS says that with treatment most people with HIV can live a long and healthy life. The NHS and Terrence Higgins Trust both say that a person on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV on.
causes: Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, a virus that attacks the immune system.
The virus passes on when certain body fluids, such as blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk, reach another person's bloodstream or mucous membranes.
It can also be passed on by sharing needles.
It can pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding.
riskFactors: Sex without a condom, since the NHS says condoms are the most effective protection against HIV during sexual contact.
Sharing needles or other injecting equipment.
For a baby, being born to a mother who has a detectable viral load, or being breastfed by her.
signs: Swollen glands and a skin rash during the early flu-like illness.
A high temperature and sore throat during the early flu-like illness.
complications: Opportunistic infections, which are certain illnesses that can lead to an AIDS diagnosis.
Illnesses such as tuberculosis or lymphoma, which can indicate AIDS.
AIDS, the most advanced stage of HIV infection, now generally described as late-stage or advanced HIV.
Passing HIV on to a baby during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding, a chance that effective treatment lowers.
hiv.diagnosis: HIV is diagnosed with a test, which the NHS provides free of charge to anyone. Testing can be done at a sexual health clinic, a GP surgery, with a home testing kit or with a home sampling kit. Testing uses a saliva or finger-prick blood sample, and laboratory results usually take a few days. If a first test is positive, a second blood test confirms the result. A test may not pick up HIV acquired very recently, a gap called the window period, and its length differs between tests. After a recent possible exposure, a negative result may be followed by a repeat test a few weeks later.
hiv.treatment: HIV is treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from copying itself in the body. These are taken every day, and the aim is an undetectable viral load. Terrence Higgins Trust recommends starting treatment straight away after diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count. HIV treatment is free on the NHS for anyone living in England.
hiv.prevention: The NHS says condoms are the most effective protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. PrEP is medicine taken by people without HIV to lower their chance of acquiring it, and it is provided free by NHS specialist sexual health services. PEP is a short course of medicine taken after a possible exposure. The NHS says sharing injecting equipment with a person who has a detectable viral load can spread HIV. The NHS also says that effective treatment with an undetectable viral load means HIV cannot be passed on to someone else.
hiv.seekCare: Anyone who thinks they may have been exposed to HIV can go to a sexual health clinic or, outside clinic hours, an A&E department, where PEP is available. NHS 111 Wales says PEP can help if started within 72 hours of possible exposure, ideally within 24 hours. A routine HIV test is available free from NHS sexual health services or a GP, or with a home kit. Terrence Higgins Trust's helpline, THT Direct, can connect people with an HIV doctor. NHS 111 can advise on urgent concerns, and 999 should be called in an emergency.

sections.heading: What is HIV, and is it the same as AIDS?
sections.body:
HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system. HIV and AIDS are not the same thing: HIV is the virus, while AIDS is the most advanced stage of infection. Without treatment, the CDC says HIV generally moves through three stages, and the last stage is AIDS. The CDC adds that progression to AIDS is now less common, and that people who take HIV treatment as prescribed may never reach it.

NHS 111 Wales says that with early diagnosis and effective treatment, most people with HIV will not develop any AIDS-related illnesses. There is currently no cure for HIV. It can be treated with antiretroviral medicines, and WHO describes it as a manageable long-term condition when prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care are available.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of HIV?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people infected with HIV have a short flu-like illness 2 to 6 weeks after infection. Common signs include a high temperature, sore throat, rash, tiredness, joint or muscle pain and swollen glands. The NHS also notes that these symptoms are commonly caused by conditions other than HIV, so they cannot show whether someone has HIV.

After this early phase, HIV may not cause any further symptoms for many years, the NHS says. An HIV test is the only way to know for sure whether someone has HIV. Terrence Higgins Trust says body fluids are highly infectious during the early weeks and months after transmission, which is one reason testing matters.

sections.heading: How is HIV passed on?
sections.body:
The NHS says that in the UK most cases of HIV are caused by sex with a person who has HIV without using a condom. Sharing needles, syringes or other equipment for injecting drugs with a person who has a detectable viral load is another route. WHO lists blood, breast milk, semen and vaginal fluids as the body fluids that carry HIV.

HIV can also pass from a mother to her baby. The NHS says this can happen during pregnancy or birth if the mother has a detectable viral load, and NHS 111 Wales lists breastfeeding as a route too.

HIV does not spread through the air like cold and flu viruses, NHS 111 Wales says. WHO states that people cannot become infected through ordinary day-to-day contact such as kissing, hugging, shaking hands or sharing personal objects, food or water. The CDC describes transmission through kissing alone as extremely rare.

sections.heading: How is HIV diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says an HIV test is the only way to confirm infection, and NHS 111 Wales says HIV testing is provided free of charge to anyone. Testing is available at sexual health clinics and GP surgeries, and home testing and home sampling kits are also available. Testing uses a saliva or finger-prick blood sample, and laboratory results usually take a few days, according to the NHS.

If a first test is positive, a second blood test is done at a clinic to confirm the result.

A test may not detect HIV acquired very recently. This gap is called the window period, and the CDC says no HIV test can detect HIV immediately after infection. After a recent possible exposure, a negative result may be followed by a repeat test a few weeks later, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: What treatment is available, and what does undetectable mean?
sections.body:
The NHS says HIV is treated with antiretroviral medicines taken every day, which stop the virus from copying itself and let the immune system recover.

The aim is an undetectable viral load, meaning the amount of virus in the blood is too low for tests to detect. The NHS says this usually takes around six months after starting treatment, and Terrence Higgins Trust says it can take up to six months for some people. Terrence Higgins Trust recommends starting treatment straight away after diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count.

The NHS says that someone on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV on to someone else. NHS 111 Wales says this applies to sex once the viral load has been undetectable for six months or more. This is known as U=U, undetectable equals untransmittable.

sections.heading: How can HIV be prevented?
sections.body:
The NHS says condoms are the most effective protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. PrEP, or pre-exposure prophylaxis, is medicine taken by people without HIV to lower their chance of acquiring it. It is provided free by NHS specialist sexual health services in England, Scotland and Wales. The NHS says it usually comes as tablets taken every day or on demand. PrEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections, an NHS sexual health service says.

PEP, or post-exposure prophylaxis, is a short course of medicine taken after a possible exposure to HIV. It is available from sexual health clinics and, outside clinic hours, A&E departments. NHS 111 Wales says it can help if started within 72 hours of possible exposure, ideally within 24 hours.

sections.heading: Living with HIV
sections.body:
The NHS says that with treatment most people with HIV can live a long and healthy life, and NHS 111 Wales describes a near-normal lifespan with early diagnosis and effective treatment. 

HIV services in England are open access, so adults with a diagnosis can refer themselves to a provider of their choice, according to the NHS England service specification. The same specification says newly diagnosed people should be assessed on the same day if they have symptoms, and within two weeks if they do not.

Terrence Higgins Trust runs a helpline, THT Direct, which can also connect someone with an HIV doctor if they do not have one yet. It also runs peer support in which every member, including the volunteers who run it, is living with HIV.

faqs.q: Is HIV the same as AIDS?
faqs.a: No. HIV is a virus, while AIDS is the most advanced stage of HIV infection. The CDC says progression to AIDS is now less common, and that people who take HIV treatment as prescribed may never reach it. NHS 111 Wales says that with early diagnosis and effective treatment most people with HIV will not develop any AIDS-related illnesses.

faqs.q: Can a person with HIV pass it on if they are on treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says that someone on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV on to someone else. NHS 111 Wales says this applies to sex once the viral load has been undetectable for six months or more. This is known as U=U, undetectable equals untransmittable. Condoms still protect against other sexually transmitted infections.

faqs.q: Can HIV be passed on by kissing or sharing food?
faqs.a: WHO states that people cannot become infected through ordinary day-to-day contact such as kissing, hugging, shaking hands or sharing food or water. The NHS says closed-mouth kissing carries no risk, and NHS 111 Wales says the virus does not spread through the air like cold and flu viruses.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for HIV?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for HIV. It can be treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from replicating. With access to effective prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care, WHO describes HIV as a manageable long-term condition that lets people live long and healthy lives.

faqs.q: Where can someone get tested for HIV?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says HIV testing is provided free of charge to anyone on the NHS. It is available at sexual health clinics and GP surgeries, and home testing and home sampling kits are also available. If a first test is positive, a second blood test confirms the result.
